Issued at 1259 AM MST Wed Nov 25 2026

It is now the day before Thanksgiving, usually the busiest travel 
day of the year. Millions of people traveling around the country to 
see loved ones to indulge in turkey and all the fixings. (I was 
never a big turkey fan, I prefer ham or steak, but each person 
has their preference).

And there is some good news on this front, especially around western 
and central Wyoming. Ridging over the Cowboy State will bring dry 
conditions and above normal temperatures to much of the area. The 
only concern will be if the fog monster can crawl out his lair this 
morning. There is little so far this morning according to satellite 
imagery as of around midnight. Some could form toward morning but my 
feeling is that is would not be as widespread as yesterday as we had 
another dry day yesterday and surface moisture is less. We will 
handle this with dense fog advisories if any develops. There will 
also be a bit of a breeze in eastern portions of the area, but in
Wyoming we call this kind of a breeze Tuesday (or Wednesday in this 
case). There could be some patchy fog again tonight, but it is 
almost impossible to pinpoint so we will leave it out of the 
forecast for now.

Thanksgiving day also looks dry, although an approaching weather 
and jet streak will begin to increase wind across portions of the 
area, although high wind is not expected.  Some lighter snow showers 
may break out across the western mountains at night, but the bulk of 
the precipitation should hold off until after sunrise Friday. With 
downsloping flow, it could also get rather mild, with highs in the 
50s possible (around 1 in 2 chance in the warmer locations). 

The real active weather starts Friday as a Pacific trough and front 
approach from the west. My personal feeling is that the current 
forecast through sunset on Friday is the wettest it will be; the 
deepest moisture likely won't arrive until Friday night into 
Saturday. There is also not a lot of cold air initially, with the 
system being of Pacific origin. We continue to have some differences 
in 700 millibar temperatures, and as a result snow levels. The GFS 
is colder by around 3 degrees celsius, but is also drier. The 
European is warmer, keeping snow levels around 7000 to 8000 feet, 
with 700 millibar temperatures between minus 1 and minus 3. This 
means western valleys may see a rain / snow mix or even a changeover 
to rain at times during the day on Friday. It still looks like the 
maximum impacts would be Friday night into Saturday though. We will 
discuss that in the next paragraph. Areas East of the Divide should 
have another mild and mainly dry day with the downsloping flow, with 
highs in the 50s possible once again. However, there could be some 
strong wind late in the day Friday in the favored northwest flow / 
cold advection locations, like Buffalo as the cold front passes. 

Friday night into Saturday still look to be the most impactful times 
in regards to travel across the area. The second and more potent 
piece of the system will move into region. The deeper moisture will 
move in with this piece of energy and bring the steadiest and 
heaviest snow. The heaviest still looks to be in the western 
mountains as well as the Bighorns with favored northwest flow 
bringing orographic enhancement. Most of these locations have at 
least a 4 out of 5 chance of 6 inches or more of snow starting 
Friday night and ending Sunday morning. There are some areas of a 
greater than 1 in 2 chance of a foot of new snow but these are 
mainly above most pass level (generally above 9500 feet). The 
exception is Togwotee Pass which as at least a 3 out of 5 chance of 
a foot of snow. There could be a gusty wind as well which could blow 
the snow around. If we needed Winter Storm Warnings, it would be 
here. But most of the mountains would likely need at least 
advisories. 

Uncertainty remains rather high East of the Divide though with 
details on the potential snow. The main driver of the snow will 
likely be jet dynamics, not orographics or surface low pressure. 
This means any potential snow would be of the banded variety. These 
bands are very difficult to pinpoint 24 hours out, let alone 3 days 
out. So, the details are still in flux. We also continue to have the 
problem of where the frontal boundary will set up, and how far down 
the cold air can reach. There is not as much of a spread in 700 
millibar temperatures today, but they are still between 4 and 7 
degrees celsius. Now, this is better than the 9 to 13 yesterday, but 
still too much of a spread to nail down details. The general trend 
is a bit colder. The truth will likely end up being somewhere 
in the middle though. As for potential amounts, we will turn to 
ensemble guidance to get an idea. And, this reflects that a lot will 
depend on snow levels. All areas have at least a 2 out of 5 chance
